entries.title: Middle East updates: Trump warns 'economic consequences' for nations helping Iran
entries.summary: US President Donald Trump has threatened Iran with an "economic warfare". Meanwhile, Australia summoned Israel's envoy over the 2024 death of an aid worker in an Israeli strike in Gaza. DW has the latest.
entries.content:
Iran

Trump warns 'economic consequences' for nations helping Iran

Published August 20, 2026last updated August 20, 2026

US President Donald Trump has threatened Iran with an "economic warfare". Meanwhile, Australia summoned Israel's envoy over the 2024 death of an aid worker in an Israeli strike in Gaza. DW has the latest.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • US President Donald Trump announced the "most crushing economic operation" ever against Iran
  • Trump said any country providing “any type of lifeline to Iran” will face "tremendous" economic repercussions
  • Iran's media dismissed Trump's threat

Here are the latest developments from the Iran war and the Middle East on Thursday, August 20:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section Australia 'outraged' over Israel declining to open criminal probe in World Central Kitchen deaths

Australia 'outraged' over Israel declining to open criminal probe in World Central Kitchen deaths

Australia on Thursday summoned Israel's ambassador to protest a decision by its military to not launch criminal investigations into the death of an Australian aid worker during a 2024 Israeli air strike on Gaza.

Australian national Lalzawmi "Zomi" Frankcom was among a group of seven World Central Kitchen employees killed on April 1, 2024 when their aid convoy was hit in an Israeli strike. 

The attack had drawn widespread international condemnation.

On Wednesday, the Israeli Defense Forces (IDF) said it had found no basis to probe the deaths of the charity's staff after a fact-finding and assessment procedure.

The IDF said in its report that it had mistakenly identified several individuals in the vehicles as Hamas militants and that the convoy deviated from its planned route. It concluded that "the decisions of the commanders did not raise reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct."

Australia's Foreign Minister Penny Wong, who summoned Israeli ambassador Hillel Newman, said relations with Israel were "difficult" after the decision.

"This decision falls far short ​of the accountability we expect," Wong said, adding that Canberra was outraged.

Wong deemed Israel's move to not launch criminal proceedings into Frankcom and her colleagues' death as "especially insulting and hurtful" as it was announced on World Humanitarian Day.

"We do not have confidence" in Israel's investigation into the killings, she said. "The Australian government will continue to keep pressing Israel for justice."

Meanwhile, Newman after meeting Wong expressed "deep sorrow and grief" to Frankcom's family as he spoke to the media.

"Israel had no intention to attack or injure in any way the aid workers that were on the convoy," he stressed.

He said that Israel's decision was that there was no "criminal liability" and went on to say: "We must respect that conclusion."

Skip next section Trump threatens Iran partners with economic punishment

Trump threatens Iran partners with economic punishment

US President Donald Trump has warned any country that supports Iran of economic consequences as war soon approaches its sixth month with no resolution in sight. 

Trump said on his Truth Social platform on Wednesday that "ANY country that allows its financial institutions, businesses, airports, or government entities to provide any type of lifeline to Iran will itself face TREMENDOUS economic consequences."

The US leader described his move as "economic warfare" and "isolation" on an unprecedented scale as he stepped up an economic pressure campaign on Iran.

"Today, I am announcing the MOST CRUSHING ECONOMIC OPERATION EVER TAKEN AGAINST ANY COUNTRY!" he said, referring to the Islamic Republic in the superlatives-embellished post.

Trump said that nobody other than him had given Tehran what he called "a greater opportunity to make a deal".

"TRAGICALLY, for them, they have failed to take it," he said.

Trump said that Washington needed the support of all its allies to isolate Iran and counter the threat posed by the country.

He compared his plan to an "ECONOMIC D-DAY".

There were no details of what Trump’s economic steps against nations supporting Iran would look like, Trump also did not mention any country by name, other than Iran.

Iran media reacts to Trump’s "economic warfare" warning

Iran’s Fars news agency on Thursday called Trump’s latest economic threat the usual "psychological warfare and propaganda campaign,"

The country’s Tasnim news agency said the US presidents' announcement was "not a new development, as the United States has been trying for years to block any financial and economic ties with Iran."

Tehran has "learned how to circumvent these restrictions and has become very skilled at doing so," Tasnim said on Telegram.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Thank you for joining us as we bring you the latest edition of our rolling updates on the war in Iran and the wider Middle Eastern crisis. 

But first here is a wrap up of the developments that took place in the region this week:

  • US President Donald Trump emphasized that no talks or conversations between Washington and Tehran were being held
  • The United Arab Emirates suspended trade ties with Iran after accusing the country of firing two ballistic missiles
  • Human Rights Watch urged the United Nations to keep its international peacekeeping force in Lebanon, saying that a decision to end UNIFIL's mandate came before this year's war and the subsequent Israeli invasion of southern Lebanon
  • The Israeli military announced criminal probes into two high-profile attacks during the Gaza war — the killings of 5-year-old Palestinian girl Hind Rajab in 2024 and 15 Palestinian paramedics in 2025

Follow along for more.

entries.title: Bangladesh lawmakers set to elect Alamgir president
entries.summary: With the ruling party holding more than a two-thirds majority in parliament, the veteran BNP politician is expected to secure the largely ceremonial presidency.
entries.content:
Bangladesh

Bangladesh lawmakers set to elect Alamgir president

August 20, 2026

With the ruling party holding more than a two-thirds majority in parliament, the veteran BNP politician is expected to secure the largely ceremonial presidency.

Bangladesh's parliament is set to elect the country's new president on Thursday, with the ruling Bangladesh Nationalist Party's (BNP) Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir widely expected to win.

The BNP holds more than a two-thirds majority in parliament, making it unlikely that retired army officer-turned-politician Oli Ahmed of the opposition Jamaat-e-Islami-led alliance will get the vote.

Lawmakers are set to vote at 2 p.m. local time (0800 UTC).

The election comes after former president Mohammed Shahabuddin, a close ally of ousted Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, resigned in July citing health concerns.

Who is Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir?

In February, Prime Minister Tarique Rahman's BNP won a landslide victory in the first election since Hasina's 2024 ouster.

The party is expected to use its majority to hand the 78-year-old Alamgir the largely ceremonial presidency.

"I never thought that I would become the president, it is the infinite grace of the party and almighty Allah," he told reporters on Tuesday, according to the state news agency BSS.

"Even after becoming president, I wish to remain beside the people and serve them."

Alamgir was repeatedly arrested under Hasina's government, facing dozens of charges he said were politically motivated.

He has been hailed in the media for "keeping the BNP organized and maintaining the party's political presence during difficult times," referring to Hasina's rule.

Edited by: Zac Crellin

entries.title: Harry and Meghan moving back to Britain: reports
entries.summary: Prince Harry and Meghan Markle will return to the UK after living in the US for over six years, according to reports. The former senior royals will reportedly live in a private residence.
entries.content:
United Kingdom

Harry and Meghan moving back to Britain: reports

August 20, 2026

Prince Harry and Meghan Markle will return to the UK after living in the US for over six years, according to reports. The former senior royals will reportedly live in a private residence.

Prince Harry and his wife Meghan are moving back to the United Kingdom more than six years after they stepped down from their royal duties and shifted base to the United States, British press reported late Wednesday.

According to The Telegraph, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex are planning to go to the UK within weeks and settle in a private, non-royal house reportedly outside London.

Several news agencies later confirmed the reports.

The couple's children Prince Archie (7) and Princess Lilibet (5) have already enrolled in a British school and will begin classes from September, the BBC and several other news outlets said in their reports.,

There is yet to be an official statement from Harry or Buckingham Palace, which historically refrains from commenting on speculation about non-working members of the royal family.

Fairytale union to bitter split from royal family

 Harry (41)  —  who is the youngest son of King Charles III and Diana, Princess of Wales — married former US actress Meghan Markle (45) in 2018 amid a media frenzy.

At the time, Harry's marriage to Meghan, who is biracial, was seen as a sign of progress within the British royal family.

However, what followed was constant friction with the monarchy, amid deep media scrutiny, which culminated into

The couple moved to California after stepping down from their duties as working royals in 2020.

The growing rift with the royal family only worsened after Harry published his memoir "Spare".

Harry and Meghan have frequently criticized the monarchy and the royal family, including in a series of TV interviews and a Netflix documentary.

They said they left Britain to escape the restrictions of royal life. The couple has also called out palace officials for being insensitive to Meghan's mental health.

In an interview with Oprah Winfrey, Meghan accused an unnamed member of the royal family of raising concerns about how dark the color of her son Archie's skin would be when she was pregnant with him.

Will Harry and Meghan's surprise move usher royal reconciliation?

Harry's relationship with his father King Charles III and his elder brother and heir-to-the-throne Prince William saw a total breakdown in the aftermath of the couple's exit. It is understood that the royal brothers are effectively estranged.

Last year, Harry said he wanted to reconcile with his father, who is undergoing treatment for cancer.

Harry and Meghan made a brief trip to the UK in early July with their two children, during which they had a private meeting with King Charles.

It was the first time Archie and Lilibet met their grandfather since the 2022 platinum jubilee of late Queen Elizabeth II.

British media reports that King Charles only became aware of Harry's plans to move back to the UK on Sunday.

Edited by: Rana Taha

entries.title: Ukraine: Several killed in fresh Russian strikes on Kyiv
entries.summary: The strikes on the Ukrainian capital and its surrounding regions also injured dozens. In neighboring Poland, the military started preventive aviation operations to protect its airspace.
entries.content:
Ukraine

Ukraine: Several killed in fresh Russian strikes on Kyiv

August 20, 2026

The strikes on the Ukrainian capital and its surrounding regions also injured dozens. In neighboring Poland, the military started preventive aviation operations to protect its airspace.

Russian strikes on the Ukrainian capital Kyiv and its surrounding regions left at least five people killed with some 23 wounded, Ukrainian authorities said in the early hours of Thursday.

Kyiv Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko said that Russia launched a ballistic missile attack on Kyiv.

What do we know about the Russian overnight attack on Kyiv?

The attack damaged residential buildings, a medical facility and an educational institution, the Kyiv city military administration said in a statement.

At least 5 people were killed in Kyiv, the administration added.

Another attack on the Brovary district in the broader Kyiv region killed one person and wounded another, Kyiv regional governor Tymur Tkachenko said.

"One industrial facility has been damaged. All relevant services are on site, working to extinguish the fire," he added.

In neighboring Poland, the Polish army said it started preventive military aviation operations to protect its airspace amid the Russian strikes. The Polish military often takes this measure amid heavy Russian strikes on Ukraine.

In Romania, the Defense Ministry said a drone crashed into an uninhabited area of the country of Tulcea during the Russian attacks.

Russia has stepped up attacks on the Ukrainian capital in recent month, with Ukraine also increasing attacks deep within Russia.

Edited by: Dharvi Vaid

entries.title: Kenya: Helicopter crash kills 7, including Ecuador spy boss
entries.summary: Six passengers — five US citizens and Ecuador's intel boss — all died in a remote area of Kenya on Wednesday when their helicopter crashed. Aviation accidents in Kenya have increased as tourism expands in the country.
entries.content:
United States of America

Kenya: Helicopter crash kills 7, including Ecuador spy boss

August 20, 2026

Six passengers — five US citizens and Ecuador's intel boss — all died in a remote area of Kenya on Wednesday when their helicopter crashed. Aviation accidents in Kenya have increased as tourism expands in the country.

Authorities in Kenya say that all seven people on board a safari helicopter — six passengers and a pilot — were killed on Wednesday when the chopper crashed in the foothills of the popular but remote tourist destination, Mount Ololokwe.

Kenya's Civil Aviation Authority said the group's Eurocopter EC130 B4 helicopter crashed at 9:13 a.m. (0613 GMT) after departing the Loisaba wildlife reserve on route to the Ewaso Nyiro area in Samburu County north of the Kenyan capital, Nairobi, adding that an investigation is underway to determine the cause of the crash.

Video footage on social media showed the smoking wreckage of the helicopter strewn about, smoldering and burning in thickly wooded terrain.

What do we know about the victims of the Kenya crash?

The US State Department said that five of the six passengers killed were US citizens.

"The US Embassy is in touch with local authorities and is providing consular assistance," read a statement. "We extend our deepest condolences to the families and loved ones on their loss."

An executive at Telemundo — a US-based Spanish-language television channel owned by Comcast/NBCUniversal — was reportedly among the victims.

Michele Sensi-Contugi, director of Ecuador's Strategic Intelligence Center was as well, and so was his wife, who also held US citizenship.

Sensi-Contugi, a former businessman, was a close friend and associate of Ecuador's right-wing President Daniel Noboa, who appointed him head of national intelligence in 2024.

"In this moment of deep sorrow, the government extends its heartfelt condolences to his family, loved ones and close associates," Ecuador's presidency said in a statement on X.

More accidents as tourism grows

Numerous travel companies offer helicopter tours to remote places like Mount Ololokwe.

But as Kenya's tourism sector has grown, so, too, has the frequency of helicopter crashes.

In February, another chopper went down in the wilderness, killing all six on board, including a parliamentarian.

Edited by: Rana Taha

entries.title: ICC slams US sanctions on court as 'flagrant attack'
entries.summary: US President Donald Trump's administration has ramped up its pressure on the International Criminal Court (ICC), accusing it of being "politicized." The EU, France, Germany, Spain and Japan have defended the court.
entries.content:
United States of America

ICC slams US sanctions on court as 'flagrant attack'

August 19, 2026

US President Donald Trump's administration has ramped up its pressure on the International Criminal Court (ICC), accusing it of being "politicized." The EU, France, Germany, Spain and Japan have defended the court.

The International Criminal Court (ICC) on Wednesday condemned US sanctions against the body's president, President Tomoko Akane of Japan, and trial lawyer Abdoulaye Seye of Senegal.

"These sanctions are a flagrant attack against the independence of an impartial judicial institution," the Hague-based court said in a statement.

It said that the US sanctions "undermine the rule of law" and jeopardize the international legal order.

The court stressed it would "continue to fully discharge its mandate with independence and impartiality, in full accordance with the Rome Statute and in the interest of victims of international crimes."

Though the United States signed in 2000 the Rome Statute that established the court in 2002, it never ratified it and under President Donald Trump, Washington accuses the court of being "politicized."

The ICC prosecutes war crimes, genocide and crimes against humanity.

EU, Japan show support for ICC

The European Union and several of its member states threw their weight behind the ICC.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa said they "stand firmly" with the court in identical statements on their X accounts.

"The ICC helps deliver justice to the victims of some of the world's most horrific crimes," they said. "To carry out this essential work, its judges and officials must be able to act independently and without external pressure."

Meanwhile, German Justice Minister Stefanie Hubig said she considered it "deeply distressing that it is the US of all countries that is launching a frontal attack on international criminal law."

She pointed out that the US helped establish the concept of international criminal law in the Nuremberg trials against members of Germany's Nazi regime.

"These US sanctions reflect contempt for the idea of the rule of law that cannot be reconciled with this tradition."

France also condemned the sanctions in a Wednesday statement.

"France condemns all ​of threats and means of coercion taken against the ​Court, its staff and the civil ⁠society organizations ​which support ​it," a statement from the spokesperson of the French Foreign Ministry said.

"France expresses its solidarity toward those magistrates targeted," it said.

Japanese Foreign Ministry Press Secretary Toshihiro Kitamura described the sanctions as "very unfortunate."

Japan is the biggest funder of the court.

The US sanctions were also condemned by the Netherlands, which hosts the court, and Spain, as well as the United Nations.

Why did the United States sanction the ICC?

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced the sanctions on Tuesday, saying he was acting under authority of an executive order signed by President Trump.

He described the measure as part of an "unwavering mission to protect Americans from this sham of a court."

"These individuals," said Rubio, "have directly engaged in efforts by the ICC to investigate, arrest, detain, or prosecute officials whose government has not consented to ICC ."

Last month, Rubio said the Trump administration would step up its efforts to dismantle the ICC, including a diplomatic campaign for other countries to leave the court.

In 2024, the ICC issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant.

The move was condemned by the United States, with Trump accusing the court of "illegitimate and baseless actions targeting America and our close ally Israel." Like the US, Israel has also never ratified the Rome Statute and is therefore not an ICC state party.

The court also issued or planned to issue arrest warrants for several now deceased Hamas leading officials.

Edited by: Rana Taha

entries.title: Ceuta: Madrid to transfer 500 vulnerable youths to mainland
entries.summary: Spanish officials have come up with a plan to transfer unaccompanied youth in the exclave Ceuta to mainland Spain. Mostly girls, they will be placed in foster homes as well as under government care.
entries.content:
August 19, 2026

Spanish officials have come up with a plan to transfer unaccompanied youth in the exclave Ceuta to mainland Spain. Mostly girls, they will be placed in foster homes as well as under government care.

Spanish immigration and youth services officials have come up with a plan to transfer roughly 500 particularly vulnerable unaccompanied youths from the North African Spanish exclave of Ceuta to mainland Spain.

Spain's Ministry of Youth and Children says the plan has a mechanism that will allow "child protection organizations to take in and care for the most vulnerable individuals — including girls — in adapted facilities on the mainland, without the need to transfer custody to [regional authorities]."

What else do we know about the measure?

On Wednesday, Spain's Migration Minister Elma Saiz told public broadcaster RNE that Madrid is working with Ceuta and Spain's regional governments to organize the transfer and placement of the children, mainly girls, in foster homes as well as under government care.

Spain's EFE news agency quoted government officials saying that a royal decree would establish "the binding and solidarity-based reception of minors by all regions."

Migration Minister Saiz emphasized the fact that the "overriding welfare of the children" must be protected at all cost.

UNICEF Spain's Lara Contreras said the approach would see Ceuta retain legal guardianship of the girls until they were transferred to child protection organizations "willing to take them in" on the Spanish mainland.

Contreras said that 97 of the 500 girls selected — aged 9 to 17 — have already been moved to improved facilities and will be transferred as soon as possible.

Contreras says it is "urgent" that authorities properly identify unaccompanied children and denounced the fact that "hundreds of them are wandering the streets alone, in unsanitary conditions."

What is the situation in Ceuta?

The children are among the roughly 80,000 individuals who crossed into Ceuta from Morocco on July 30 in hopes of starting a better life in Europe.

Though most migrants have since returned to Morocco, Spanish Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska recently said that around 5,000 remain in Ceuta.

Spain's national police have reportedly identified 2,168 unaccompanied minors living on the streets since the border crossing and handed them over to local authorities on July 30.

Edited by: Saim Dušan Inayatullah

entries.title: Zambia: Mundubile seeks to overturn election result in court
entries.summary: Zambian opposition leader Brian Mundubile's party alleges shots were fired during a raid of his house on election night. UN rights chief Volker Türk called for Zambia to stop arresting people "arbitrarily."
entries.content:
Zambia

Zambia: Mundubile seeks to overturn election result in court

August 19, 2026

Zambian opposition leader Brian Mundubile's party alleges shots were fired during a raid of his house on election night. UN rights chief Volker Türk called for Zambia to stop arresting people "arbitrarily."

Zambian opposition leader Brian Mundubile said on Wednesday that he plans to challenge the results of this month's presidential election result in court.

Zambia's electoral commission declared incumbent President Hakainde Hichilema the winner of the election on Tuesday, giving him a second five-year term. He has been in power since 2021.

The election was marred by accusations of interference and by arrests of opposition figures.

What did Mundubile say about his push to challenge the election result?

While announcing his intention to legally challenge the result, Mundubile pointed to irregularities and other issues with the election.

"Our campaign ​has documented serious irregularities, inconsistencies and circumstances ​surrounding the conduct, counting, transmission and declaration of results", Mundubile said in a statement issued from an undisclosed location.

The politician had earlier said he was under protection due to threats.

Mundubile received 38% of the vote on Tuesday, while Hichilema took 60%, according to the electoral commission.

While the vote itself was largely peaceful, some 11 people — including leading figures in the opposition — were arrested on the night of the election. The government said that the arrests were part of a raid against "militia activity.”

Mundubile's National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP) said that shots were fired during the raid of the opposition figure's home. The party also denied any ties to militias.

Vote counting was also suspended for multiple hours on Friday after the electoral commission reported attacks against polling officials and theft of some ballots.

UN rights chief calls for Zambia to halt arrests, EU mission notes irregularity

The United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, Volker Türk, said he was concerned by reports of arrests of opposition members.

In a statement, he urged authorities "to stop arresting people arbitrarily and to uphold fully the due process rights of all those detained."

Meanwhile, an electoral observer mission for the European Union raised concerns around transparency.

"Observers reported extended breaks during the results tabulation process in almost half of observations, as the returning officers seemed to wait and receive instructions from... headquarters before announcing results," the mission said.

Edited by: Mark Hallam

entries.title: Liberia says it's taking in 1,200 third-country US deportees
entries.summary: The government in Monrovia says the first batch of 20 people should arrive in Liberia on Thursday. The Trump administration has been seeking countries to take people it cannot send back to their countries of origin.
entries.content:
United States of America

Liberia says it's taking in 1,200 third-country US deportees

August 19, 2026

The government in Monrovia says the first batch of 20 people should arrive in Liberia on Thursday. The Trump administration has been seeking countries to take people it cannot send back to their countries of origin.

Liberia has agreed to accept up to 1,200 third-country deportees from the United States in the next 12 months, the government said this week. 

It said that the first group of 20 were expected to arrive on Thursday.

Donald Trump's administration has recently struck several deals with African countries to take in people it cannot legally send back to their home countries — typically because of US court orders ruling that doing so would put them in danger. 

What did Liberia say about the agreement?

"Liberia intends to accept up to 1,200 persons to be transferred from the United States of America within a year," the Liberian government said in a statement published on Tuesday.

It said that the people would be received "as guests" and that they would be "free to depart the country when they so desire" or to apply for asylum.

The government's statement said the deportees "will include citizens or nationals of ‌African ​and Western Hemisphere countries who are medically authorized to travel."

It said that the deal did not involve a quid pro quo with the US and that it was not demanding and had not received any direct compensation.

However, it also said that it would receive "support to help manage the program and strengthen its migration system more broadly," without elaborating.

The statement also referenced Liberia's 19th century history as a refuge for freed slaves from the US, and its "long history of accepting ⁠people seeking refuge from political ​and other crises."

Why is the US looking for support of this kind from African countries?

The announcement follows around a year after Liberian President Joseph Boakai visited the White House among a group of African leaders and held talks with Trump. 

Seeking a way to deport would-be migrants that it cannot send back to their countries of origin — very often because of US courts ruling that doing so would put them at risk of torture or other abuses — the Trump administration has been seeking agreements with third countries willing to take some of the people.

The US government has defended such agreements as lawful, although some rights groups and advocates have said the details are often opaque and that many of the deportees are ultimately repatriated.

Beyond Monrovia's description, no information was immediately available on where exactly the deportees hailed from.

Other African countries including the Democratic Republic of Congo, the Central African Republic, Equatorian Guinea, Cameroon, Ghana and Sierra Leone have reached similar accords with the US. 

The EU is currently looking into somewhat comparable plans that would allow member states to send rejected asylum seekers to so-called "return hubs" in third countries as part of bilateral or multilateral agreements, provided various conditions were met.

Edited by: Saim Dušan Inayatullah

entries.title: CAR: Scores killed in landslide at illegal gold mine
entries.summary: More than 100 workers may have been killed in a landslide at an illegal mine near the Central African Republic's border with Cameroon, say authorities. More miners are trapped and hope for their survival is fading.
entries.content:
Africa

CAR: Scores killed in landslide at illegal gold mine

August 19, 2026

More than 100 workers may have been killed in a landslide at an illegal mine near the Central African Republic's border with Cameroon, say authorities. More miners are trapped and hope for their survival is fading.

Authorities in the western part of the Central African Republic (CAR) say dozens of laborers were killed Tuesday afternoon when a landslide buried them at the illegal Zamboye mining site near the Cameroon border — about 50 kilometers (31 miles) from the town of Baboua.

Death tolls have ranged from "at least 30" initially to "over 100," with local authorities saying the window for survival is quickly closing for the many miners still buried at the site.

Video uploaded to social media platforms showed bodies churning in earth as the landslide lunges into the open-pit site beneath, burying everything in its path.

Frantic rescue activities continued on Wednesday with reports of mud-covered young men and women pulling bodies from the mine's collapsed entrance, as still more screamed for help.

"The collapse of several underground tunnels in which miners were operating," was given as the cause of the collapse by the Baboua public prosecutor's office, which also announced that an investigation had been launched.

CAR government spokesman Evariste Ngamana expressed sympathy and pledged the government was "working hard to provide relief and assistance."

What is the state of CAR's 'artisanal' mines?

Improvised "artisanal" mines in the gold-rich region are often illegal and shoddily built, following limited or no safety standards whatsoever.

That means the thousands of laborers who use their hands to mine for gold every day, put their lives at risk each time they enter one.

Serious accidents are a regular occurrence and these are usually very deadly.

Dozens of miners have been killed in landslides in the area since the beginning of the year.

Edited by: Saim Dušan Inayatullah
